title: The Sharpe Pint: Mayfair's Tax Blow, the Death of the Overnight Drift, and the Itô Tax

opening_mood.text: Morning. We have officially crossed into the second half of 2026, and the City is nursing a mild Q2 hangover. After wrapping up the best quarter since 2020, the markets are taking a breather, but there is absolutely no quiet summer lull in sight. Today, we are looking at a massive tax blow for Mayfair's elite, a hard deadline for crypto, and Zuck turning his expensive AI hobby into a proper cloud business. Grab a flat white, find a quiet corner, and let's get you sharp for the day.

content.text: BlueCrest's £200m Supreme Court Tax Blow

Michael Platt's BlueCrest Capital Management has lost a £200 million ($265 million) battle with HMRC in the UK Supreme Court. The court unanimously rejected BlueCrest's appeal, ruling that discretionary payouts to senior traders were actually 'disguised salary' rather than partnership profit shares, making them subject to normal income tax. BlueCrest didn't take it lying down, declaring that the UK is 'no longer a serious contender' for doing business.

Why it matters: The Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) structure has been the holy grail of tax efficiency for London hedge funds and boutique advisory shops. By paying top performers as partners sharing in profits, firms avoided hefty National Insurance contributions and top-rate income tax. The Supreme Court has effectively blown this up, ruling that if a trader's payout is discretionary and based on individual performance rather than overall firm profits, it is a salary.

The City angle: This is a massive headache for Mayfair. It follows XTX Markets founder Alex Gerko losing a similar tax case, signalling a coordinated HMRC crackdown on City pay structures. Expect to see hedge funds scrambling to restructure their compensation models, potentially accelerating the brain drain to Dubai, Geneva, or Singapore.

What to say at the pub: 'The BlueCrest ruling is a killer for the classic LLP loophole. If you cannot pay traders tax-efficiently based on their individual book, the whole Mayfair partnership model starts to look a bit shaky. Don't be surprised if we see more PMs packing their bags for Abu Dhabi.'
The FCA Fires the Starting Gun on UK Crypto Regulation

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has finally published its complete, comprehensive digital assets regime, bringing three years of policy development to a close. The framework spans stablecoin issuance, trading, custody, staking, and market abuse. The catch? The application window for authorisation opens on 30 September 2026 and slams shut on 28 February 2027. Any firm that misses the deadline must halt UK operations immediately.

Why it matters: This is the UK's answer to Europe's MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets) regulation. It is a hard, unforgiving deadline. Crucially, the FCA has made it clear that existing Money Laundering Regulations (MLR) registrations do not automatically carry over. Even established players must submit a fresh, highly detailed application to survive.

The City angle: Compliance and legal departments at London's quant shops and crypto brokers are going to be working overtime. It forces a rapid professionalisation of the UK crypto scene, but the tight timeline means some smaller players will inevitably get squeezed out or forced to relocate.

What to say in an interview: 'The FCA's new digital assets regime is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it provides the regulatory certainty institutional investors need to commit capital. On the other, the five-month application window is incredibly tight, and the refusal to grandfather in existing MLR registrations shows the FCA is playing hardball.'
Meta Turns an AI Cost Centre into a Revenue Engine

Meta Platforms' stock surged 9.27% on Wednesday, recovering a massive chunk of its June losses, after the company announced 'Meta Compute'. The new service will rent out Meta's excess AI computing infrastructure to outside customers, turning its massive capex bill into a direct revenue stream.

Why it matters: For the past year, the market's biggest worry about the 'Magnificent Seven' has been their eye-watering capital expenditure on AI chips and data centres. Meta's move directly addresses this by showing how it can monetise its excess capacity. It also puts Meta in direct competition with AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and specialised GPU clouds like CoreWeave (which tumbled 14% on the news).

The City angle: This is a major shift in the hyperscaler dynamic. If Meta can successfully monetise its infrastructure, it changes the ROI calculations for AI capex and could force other tech giants to follow suit. It also shows that the market is desperate for tangible AI monetisation angles beyond just 'better chatbots.'

What to say at work: 'Meta renting out its excess compute is a brilliant way to de-risk its capex. It essentially turns an expensive infrastructure bet into a flexible utility business. It is a massive warning shot to specialised GPU clouds like CoreWeave, who suddenly have to compete with Meta's scale.'
Michael Burry's 'Big Short' Targets the AI Elite

The 'Big Short' himself, Michael Burry of Scion Asset Management, is back. Regulatory disclosures and market reports reveal that Burry has taken short positions against several AI leaders, including Nvidia and Applied Materials. The news, combined with profit-taking, triggered a sharp selloff in chipmakers, with Micron and SanDisk plummeting 11% and South Korea's Kospi index dropping nearly 8%.

Why it matters: Burry's endorsement of the 'AI bubble' thesis gives institutional bears a highly visible rallying cry. While the AI momentum trade has been unstoppable, the fundamentals of chip demand vs. supply are starting to look stretched, and memory stocks are taking the brunt of the profit-taking.

The City angle: For long/short equity funds and asset managers, this is the classic valuation vs. momentum battle. If Burry is right, the tech rotation we have been seeing in recent weeks could accelerate into a broader market correction.

What to say in an interview: 'Burry shorting Nvidia and Applied Materials is the ultimate contrarian play. While the long-term potential of AI is real, the short-term valuation multiples assume flawless execution and infinite demand. The double-digit drops in memory stocks like Micron suggest that some investors are starting to agree with him and lock in profits.'
SoftBank's 10-Gigawatt Power Play

SoftBank Corp. and SoftBank Group Corp. have announced the establishment of 'SB Neo' in the US. The new entity will operate a 'neocloud' business leveraging SoftBank's massive 10-gigawatt-scale energy and AI infrastructure currently under development. It plans to launch services by FY2027 to provide major US enterprises and hyperscalers with the computing power needed for large-scale AI training.

Why it matters: The bottleneck for AI is no longer just securing Nvidia chips; it is securing the electricity to run them. A 10-gigawatt power capacity is absolutely gargantuan—enough to power millions of homes. SoftBank is positioning itself not just as a tech investor, but as the ultimate power-and-compute landlord.

The City angle: This highlights how the AI trade is shifting from pure software and hardware to infrastructure, energy, and utilities. Private credit and infrastructure funds are heavily funding these massive power plays, which offer long-term, inflation-protected cash flows.

What to say at work: 'SoftBank's SB Neo is a massive bet on the physical constraints of AI. By securing 10 gigawatts of power capacity, they are tackling the real bottleneck of the AI race: electricity. It is less of a tech play and more of an infrastructure and utility play.'
The AI Headcount Cull is Showing Up in Macro Data

While the overall US labour market remains robust, a quiet cull is happening in high-paying white-collar sectors. A new report highlights that the financial-activities and information sectors are losing an average of 28,000 jobs monthly in 2026, driven by rapid AI adoption. Layoff tracker Challenger, Gray & Christmas found almost 102,000 announced job cuts attributed to AI so far this year, with tech and finance bearing the brunt.

Why it matters: This is the first clear, macro-level evidence of AI-driven job displacement in high-paying white-collar sectors. We have spent two years talking about AI productivity; now we are seeing the headcount reduction.

The City angle: For banks and asset managers, this shows the 'efficiency' side of the AI investment is actually starting to hit the bottom line (lower headcount costs), but it also raises questions about long-term talent pipelines. If you automate away the entry-level analyst roles, where do the future VPs and MDs learn the trade?

What to say in an interview: 'The loss of 28,000 jobs a month in finance and tech is a structural shift. It is great for operating margins in the short term, but it means the entry-level roles where people actually learn the trade are disappearing. Firms will need to rethink how they train and develop junior talent in an AI-driven environment.'
Kevin Warsh's Sintra Debut and the 'Family Fight'

New Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh made his first global appearance at the ECB's Sintra forum. He signalled optimism on US growth potential and noted that inflation risks are fading, but reiterated his commitment to restoring price stability. He also teased a 'good family fight' at the upcoming July FOMC meeting.

Why it matters: Warsh is the new Fed Chair under the Trump administration. Markets are closely watching his tone to see if he will be more hawkish or dovish, and how independent the Fed will remain. His comments helped push the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.48% as markets digested his outlook ahead of the nonfarm payrolls.

The City angle: Macro traders and fixed-income desks are trying to price the 'Warsh Fed'. The mention of a 'good family fight' in July suggests the FOMC is highly divided on the next move, which means we should expect more volatility in the front end of the curve.

What to say at work: 'Warsh's debut at Sintra shows he is trying to walk a tightrope—optimistic on growth but firm on inflation. The mention of a "family fight" in July suggests the FOMC is highly divided, so we should expect a lot more volatility in the front end of the curve as the market tries to price his next move.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Q2 Hangover and Sintra Spoilers

After wrapping up the best quarter since 2020, Wall Street opened the second half of the year with a classic morning-after headache. The S&P 500 slipped 0.22% to 7,483.23, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 0.66% to 26,040.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average teased us by hitting a fresh intraday record high before finishing essentially flat, down a mere 0.03% to 52,305.24. In short, it is a bit of book-clearing and profit-taking after a historic run, rather than a structural panic.

But the real action was under the hood. Meta Platforms was the absolute star of the session, surging 9.27%—its best day in five months—on the announcement of 'Meta Compute'. Essentially, Zuck is going to rent out Meta’s massive AI computing infrastructure to third parties. This is a brilliant narrative shift: it repositions Meta from an AI capex black hole into a high-margin cloud revenue engine. Palantir also climbed 8% on a fresh deal with Nvidia. However, the rest of the chip sector looked like a crime scene. Micron and SanDisk both plummeted 11%, and infrastructure player CoreWeave tumbled 14%. The catalyst? A mix of valuation jitters and rumours that Michael Burry has put on shorts against several AI darlings, including Nvidia.
Warsh’s Sintra Cold Shower

Over in Portugal, the ECB’s Sintra forum provided the macro drama of the week. The newly minted Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh, took the stage and immediately threw cold water on any hopes of a central bank pivot. Warsh declared he would 'disappoint' anyone who thinks he will tolerate inflation above 2%, making it clear that Donald Trump’s public demands for rate cuts will fall on deaf ears. He also rejected the concept of forward guidance, telling markets to focus on hard economic data rather than expecting the Fed to hold their hands. The bond market got the message: the US 10-year Treasury yield marched up to 4.48%.

Speaking of data, the US labour market is playing a game of mixed signals. June’s ADP private payrolls came in soft at 98,000 (well below the 118,000 expected). Yet, the May JOLTS report showed job openings unexpectedly spiked to a two-year high of 7.59 million. This sets up a massive clash for today’s Non-Farm Payrolls (NFP) report, which has been pulled forward to Thursday because of the July 4th long weekend. If NFP comes in hot, expect Warsh’s hawkishness to look very justified, and yields to climb further.
Yen Watch, Cheap Oil, and State Street’s Big Win

items: **The Yen’s 40-Year Low:** The Japanese Yen weakened to a fresh 40-year low of 162.84 against the dollar. Tokyo is on high alert for intervention. The cross-asset risk here is real: Japan holds over $1.2 trillion in US Treasuries. If they have to liquidate some of those holdings to defend the Yen, it could send US yields spiking even higher.

**Oil Slides on Peace Hopes:** Brent crude slid to $71.57 and WTI to $68.77—both multi-month lows. Markets are pricing in a potential breakthrough in US-Iran peace talks that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Cheaper energy is a massive relief valve for global inflation, even if Warsh won't admit it yet.

**State Street’s Golden Ticket:** In a major structural development, the US Treasury announced the investment lineup for the highly anticipated 'Trump Accounts' (custodial IRAs for kids launching July 4). State Street’s SPDR Portfolio S&P 500 ETF (SPYM) was selected as the exclusive default fund. With over 6 million sign-ups already, this is an absolute asset-gathering coup for State Street.

sections.title: Financial Idea: The Working Capital Peg

content.text: The Working Capital Peg: How Not to Get Stitched Up in M&A

When you buy a business, the headline press release always shouts about the "Enterprise Value"—say, £100 million on a "cash-free, debt-free" basis. It sounds clean. The seller keeps the cash in the bank, pays off their bank loans, and hands you the keys. But if you aren't careful, you might walk into your newly acquired company on Monday morning only to find the cupboards are bare, the suppliers are striking because they haven't been paid in months, and customers are refusing to pay because they were bullied into prepaying their invoices three weeks ago.

To prevent this, M&A professionals use a mechanism called the Net Working Capital (NWC) Peg. It is the financial equivalent of making sure the seller doesn't empty the beer cellar before handing over the keys to the pub.
The Concept: What is the NWC Peg?

Net Working Capital is the operational fuel of a business—essentially, Current Assets (like inventory and accounts receivable) minus Current Liabilities (like accounts payable and accrued expenses), excluding cash and debt. The NWC Peg is a mutually agreed-upon "target" or "normal" level of working capital that the seller must deliver at the exact moment the deal closes. It is typically calculated as a trailing 12-month (TTM) average of the company's working capital, adjusted to strip out any weird, one-off anomalies (a process called "normalisation").
A Simple Example: The Dollar-for-Dollar Adjustment

Let’s say you agree to buy a widget manufacturer for a headline price of £100 million. After digging through the books, your due diligence team agrees that the business needs a "normal" working capital level of £10 million to run day-to-day. This £10 million becomes your Peg. When the deal actually closes, the accountants draw up a "closing balance sheet" to measure the actual NWC left in the business. This triggers a dollar-for-dollar adjustment to the final purchase price:

items: Scenario A (The Starved Business): The seller stopped paying their suppliers and let inventory run down to zero to hoard cash before closing. The actual NWC at close is only £7 million. Because they left you £3 million short of the Peg, you deduct £3 million from the purchase price. You pay £97 million, using the saved £3 million to restock the shelves and pay the angry suppliers.

Scenario B (The Overfunded Business): The seller paid off suppliers early and built up extra inventory. The actual NWC at close is £12 million. Because they left you £2 million of extra operational value, you pay them £102 million.

content.text: Why It Matters in Asset Management and Private Equity

In private equity, the NWC Peg is a massive, high-stakes battleground. Because the adjustment is settled dollar-for-dollar at closing, a £1 million shift in the Peg has the exact same impact on your returns as a £1 million shift in the enterprise value. Sellers will try to inflate the Peg if they expect working capital to rise, or depress it if they want to sweep more cash. Furthermore, if the business is highly seasonal (like a toy retailer or an ice cream brand), using a simple 12-month average can be disastrous if the deal closes at the peak or trough of the cycle. If you close an ice cream business in July, its working capital will be naturally massive (tons of inventory and receivables). If you set the Peg based on a flat annual average, the buyer will end up paying a massive upward adjustment to the seller, only to watch that working capital evaporate as winter approaches.
Common Beginner Mistakes

The most common rookie mistake is confusing "Working Capital" with "Cash." Beginners often think that because a deal is "cash-free," the seller can just sweep the bank accounts and leave the business with zero working capital. But a business cannot run with zero working capital. If you have £0 of receivables and inventory, and £0 of payables, your business is dead. The seller sweeps the cash, but they must leave the operating assets and liabilities behind.
How to Ace This in an Interview

If you are interviewing for investment banking, private equity, or corporate development, this is a classic way to show you aren't just a textbook-memorising robot. When asked to walk from Enterprise Value to Equity Value, don't just stop at "minus debt, plus cash." Add this kicker:

"And finally, you adjust for any deviation between the actual Net Working Capital at closing and the agreed Net Working Capital Peg. If actual NWC is below the Peg, it’s a reduction to the purchase price; if it’s above, it’s an increase."

If they ask how a seller might try to "game" a transaction in the final weeks, you can explain that a seller might try to stretch payables (delaying payments to suppliers to keep cash on their balance sheet) or accelerate collections (offering discounts to customers to pay early). This inflates the cash they get to keep, while dragging down the working capital. A robust NWC Peg and a post-closing adjustment mechanism are the buyer's only shield against this kind of value leakage.
Over a Pint: The Discussion Point

Next time you're talking deals, ask your colleagues: "How are we structuring the working capital peg on our current pipeline? Are we using a standard 12-month average, or are we adjusting for the recent inflation in input costs?" Because if supplier costs have jumped 15% in the last six months, a historical 12-month average Peg will be artificially low, meaning the buyer will get caught short on Day 1 and have to fund the gap out of their own pocket.

sections.title: Quant & AI: The Itô Tax and B-NRDEs

content.text: The Problem with Standard Signatures: The Itô Tax

If you have spent any time looking at deep learning for time series, you have probably run into path signatures. They are brilliant mathematical tools from rough path theory that compress a messy, irregularly sampled price path into a neat set of geometric statistics. But there is a massive, silent tax that quant finance has been paying to use them. Standard signatures are built on Stratonovich calculus, which obeys the standard chain rule. Finance, however, runs on Itô calculus. In Itô's world, we have quadratic variation—that extra d[X, X] term from Itô's Lemma that captures volatility clustering and path variance.

To force standard signatures to see this quadratic variation, quants have to use a clunky hack called 'lead-lag lifting'. This involves doubling the time steps and doubling the feature dimensions by lagging the path against itself. It works, but it is computationally expensive and feels like putting diesel in a Tesla. Furthermore, if you are modelling dynamics on curved spaces—like predicting covariance matrices, which must live on the manifold of Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) matrices—standard signatures completely fall apart because the curvature makes repeated derivatives order-dependent.
The Idea: Branched Neural Rough Differential Equations (B-NRDEs)

Enter a fresh paper from ICML 2026 by Luke Thompson and his co-authors: 'Learning Manifold and Itô Dynamics with Branched Neural Rough Differential Equations' (B-NRDEs). Instead of trying to force Itô dynamics into a Stratonovich box, the authors redesign the underlying algebra of the neural differential equation. They swap out the standard signature for 'branched signatures' based on rooted trees:

items: Grossman-Larson rooted trees for Euclidean Itô dynamics: This mathematically captures quadratic variation natively, meaning zero lead-lag lifting is required.

Munthe-Kaas-Wright planar rooted trees for dynamics on manifolds: This allows the model to perform geometric numerical integration directly on curved spaces, ensuring predicted states never drift off their allowed boundaries.

content.text: Finance Use Case: Keeping Covariances Positive Definite

Imagine you are building a deep learning model to predict the rolling covariance matrix of a 10-asset portfolio. Covariance matrices must be Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD). If your neural network outputs a matrix that is not positive definite (even by a tiny numerical margin), your portfolio optimizer will throw a tantrum, refuse to invert the matrix, and crash your trading system. B-NRDEs allow you to model the continuous-time path of the covariance matrix directly on the SPD manifold. It guarantees that the predicted covariance matrix is mathematically valid at every single step, while natively capturing the path-dependent volatility dynamics of the underlying assets.
How It Looks in Code
Here is a conceptual comparison of how standard signatures hack Itô dynamics versus how a branched signature approach captures it natively:

# Standard Signature approach (requires lead-lag lifting to capture Itô quadratic variation)
def standard_signature_prep(path):
    # path shape: (time_steps, d)
    # Lead-lag lift doubles the dimension to (time_steps * 2, d * 2)
    lead = path[1:]
    lag = path[:-1]
    lead_lag_path = combine_lead_lag(lead, lag) 
    return signatory.signature(lead_lag_path, depth=2)

# B-NRDE approach (uses Grossman-Larson rooted trees to capture Itô dynamics natively)
class BranchedRoughPathLift:
    def __init__(self, depth=2):
        self.depth = depth
        
    def fit_transform(self, path):
        # Natively extracts tree-based features without doubling dimensions
        # Tree '.' represents the path increment (dx)
        # Tree '[., .]' represents the quadratic variation (d[X, X])
        increments = np.diff(path, axis=0)
        quad_var = np.cumsum(increments**2, axis=0) # [., .] term
        
        # Combine into a branched signature representation
        branched_features = np.concatenate([increments, quad_var], axis=-1)
        return branched_features
The Interview / Pub Conversation Angle

If you are interviewing for a systematic trading or quantitative research role, or just chatting with the desk's lead quant over a pint, bring this up. Most people who use signatures just pip-install 'signatory' or 'iisignals' and call it a day. If you can explain why standard signatures require lead-lag lifting (because they assume Stratonovich calculus and lack quadratic variation) and how branched rough paths (using Grossman-Larson trees) solve this natively, you instantly separate yourself from the crowd. It shows you actually understand the intersection of stochastic calculus and deep learning, rather than just importing PyTorch and hoping for the best.
The Catch

As with all elegant math, there is a computational tax. The paper notes that computing the quadratic variation terms scales as O(d^2), where d is the state dimension. This means B-NRDEs are currently fantastic for low-to-medium dimensional systems (like modeling a few volatility factors or a small basket of assets) but will struggle to scale to a 500-stock portfolio without some form of factor-model dimension reduction first.

sections.title: The Reading List: The Death of the Overnight Drift

content.text: The Ghost in the Machine: Why a Famous Quant Trade Just Died

If you have spent any time around a quant desk or an index-rebalancing team over the last few years, you will have heard of the 'overnight drift'. It was one of those beautiful, clean market anomalies that felt like free money. But according to a brand-new paper published by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the trade has officially flatlined. The paper, titled 'The Disappearing Overnight Drift' by Nina Boyarchenko, Lars C. Larsen, and Paul Whelan, is a brilliant, post-mortem look at what happens when the plumbing of the market shifts beneath our feet.

First, a quick refresher on the anomaly itself. Back in 2021, the authors documented a bizarre phenomenon: if you held U.S. equity futures (like S&P 500 E-minis) during the narrow window between 2:00 a.m. and 3:00 a.m. Eastern Time—exactly when European markets open—you harvested a massive, highly reliable return. This single hour accounted for roughly 3.7% annualized, or over 60% of the contract's total overnight returns. It was a massive anomaly, and naturally, everyone wanted a piece of it.

Why did it happen? It was all about inventory risk. At the U.S. close (15:15 to 16:15 ET), institutional investors often dump massive, lopsided orders. Liquidity providers (LPs) act as the buyers of last resort, absorbing this lopsided inventory and holding it overnight. Because overnight markets are thin and risky, LPs demand a steep discount at the close to compensate them for the risk. When European traders wake up a few hours later, they start buying, the price rebounds to its fair value, and the LPs pocket the difference. That rebound is the overnight drift.

But when the authors looked at the post-publication data from 2021 through 2025, they found the drift had completely vanished. The 2:00–3:00 a.m. window has averaged close to zero. To find out why, they tested three distinct channels using their inventory-risk framework.
The Three Suspects

items: Channel 1: Closing Order Imbalances. Are end-of-day institutional flows simply less lopsided than they used to be?
Channel 2: Return Variance. Has overnight volatility dropped, making it less risky for LPs to hold inventory?
Channel 3: Risk-Bearing Capacity. Have LPs become more willing or able to hold overnight risk, compressing the premium they demand?

content.text: The results are incredibly clean. It wasn't overnight volatility (the VIX barely budged, averaging 19.4 versus 20.4 historically). And it wasn't a surge in overnight liquidity capacity (overnight volume share only ticked up from 15% to 16%). Instead, the culprit was entirely Channel 1. The dispersion of end-of-day 'relative signed volume'—the lopsidedness of the final hour's trading—collapsed by more than half, from a standard deviation of 6.5% down to 2.9%. Extreme closing-imbalance days have simply vanished.
"Extreme closing-imbalance days, which the inventory-risk framework identifies as a source of overnight pricing pressure, have become markedly rarer."
Why This Matters to You

If you are in asset management, trading, or quant research, this is a masterclass in how markets evolve. The lazy explanation for a disappearing anomaly is always 'arbitrageurs read the paper and competed it away'. But this paper shows that the structural plumbing actually changed. Institutional execution algorithms have become incredibly sophisticated at smoothing out end-of-day flows, meaning LPs are rarely left holding massive, lopsided risk at the close. No risk, no discount, no drift.
What to Skim

Skip the heavy mathematical derivations of the inventory-risk model in their original 2023 journal article. Instead, go straight to the charts in this July 2026 blog post. The contrast between the lopsided overnight return curves of 2007–2020 and the completely flatlined curves of 2021–2025 is a stark, beautiful visual of a dead trade.
What to Say Over a Pint

items: If anyone tells you market anomalies are permanent, point them to the overnight drift. It went from generating 60% of futures' overnight returns to absolute zero in five years.

It's not just that 'arbitrageurs killed it.' The actual structural plumbing changed: lopsided institutional flows at the U.S. close compressed by more than half. Execution algos are getting too good at hiding their footprints.
The authors left us with a great falsifiable prediction: if closing imbalances widen out again, the drift should reappear. It's a sleeping anomaly, not necessarily a dead one.

content.text: The Peltzman Effect: Why Safety Nets Make Us Do Backflips

Imagine you are driving a car equipped with lane assist, automatic emergency braking, and ten airbags. Do you drive more cautiously? Statistically, no. You drive faster, brake later, and are far more likely to check your phone at a red light. This is the Peltzman Effect (or risk compensation), named after Chicago economist Sam Peltzman. In 1975, he published a landmark paper showing that introducing mandatory seatbelt laws in the US did not actually reduce total traffic fatalities. Why? Because drivers felt safer, so they drove more aggressively, offsetting the safety gains and putting pedestrians at greater risk.

Humans possess a subconscious "risk thermostat". If you make our environment safer, we do not just bank the safety; we "spend" it on performance, speed, or sheer laziness. We adjust our behaviour to keep our perceived risk at a comfortable, constant level.
How it plays out in the City
This is not just about seatbelts; it is the hidden engine behind some of the biggest blow-ups and operational slip-ups in finance. Consider how it manifests across different desks:

items: Portfolio Management: When a fund introduces tighter stop-losses or portfolio insurance (like put options), traders do not just sit back and relax. They think, "My downside is capped," and use that safety margin to put on much larger, more speculative, or highly correlated positions.

Banking Regulation: Deposit insurance (like the UK’s FSCS) was designed to prevent bank runs. But because depositors know their money is safe, they stop checking if a bank is run by cowboys and simply chase the highest yield. Meanwhile, banks take on riskier assets because they know the taxpayer backs the downside.

The "Senior Review" Trap: On a desk level, if you know your VP or an automated AI compliance tool is going to thoroughly review your model before it goes to the client, you subconsciously stop double-checking your own formulas. You outsource your vigilance to the safety net, which is exactly how embarrassing errors slip through when the VP is having a busy day.

content.text: How to use this at work

If you are designing risk limits, compliance processes, or project timelines, never assume a new guardrail will simply reduce risk. It won't. Your team will immediately treat the new guardrail as the new baseline and push right up against it. If you set a hard stop-loss, expect traders to trade larger. If you give a team a two-week buffer on a deadline, expect them to start the work two weeks later.

To combat this in your own career, practice "simulated soloing". When you finish a model or a pitch deck, pretend there is no VP, no compliance tool, and no safety net. If this goes straight to the client with your name on it, are you absolutely sure it is right? Force your risk thermostat back down.
The one-liner to take to the pub
"When you give people a safety net, they don't sit safely—they start doing backflips."
